text: TEMPLATE LITERALS Template literals are awesome. Here's why. Have you ever written code like this? We all have. With template literals, you can make it look like this. So with template literals, we can create multiple lines without using the escaped new line character or concatenating with the plus symbol. We can use double and single quotes freely, and we can include variables, do math calculations, or even call a function that returns a value. The key to the template literal is the backticks. That's the key just to the left of the number one key on your keyboard. Now we can format the string more naturally, making it easier to see how the output will look. To add variables, we can use a placeholder by using dollar sign curly braces. Then within the placeholder, we use an expression. This expression can be a variable, math calculation, or even a function. This is called expression interpolation. Here we are passing in the name, day, and temperature. We can also use a function to make the name uppercase if we wanted. And because the weather people sometimes don't get it right, we can do some math on the temperature. Lastly, there is something called tagged template literals. This is basically passing a template literal into a function. By doing this, we can separate the strings from the expressions and then manipulate them as needed. So here we are passing the hash symbol and two variables. We can see in the console that the function is separating the strings from the variables and creating arrays for each. We can then manipulate the data as needed. This has been a 90-second JavaScript January.
